messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened three years ago, in the parking garage beneath the county office building where Marcus worked as a social worker. A man had followed him from the stairwell, pressed a knife to his ribs, and forced him into the maintenance alcove. Marcus remembered the concrete dust on the floor, the hum of the ventilation fan, the way his own voice had sounded thin and far away when he tried to speak. He had not screamed. He had not fought. He had done exactly what the man said, and afterward, when he drove home on the expressway, his hands had not stopped shaking for two hours.

What stayed with him was not the physical memory alone—though the terror returned whole and undiminished whenever he thought of it, a wave of cold panic that left him breathless—but the shame. He could not find words for what had happened, even now. In sessions with his own therapist, he would start a sentence and stop, the shape of the event dissolving before he could hold it. He had come to believe that the fact he could not describe it meant something was wrong with him, that a real man would have fought back or at least been able to talk about it afterward.

In the months that followed, Marcus began to notice that certain spaces felt wrong. Enclosed areas—the supply closet at work, the elevator in his apartment building, the narrow hallway outside his office—made his chest tighten. He took the stairs instead, even when his knees ached. But the stairs themselves became difficult: he found himself looking behind him constantly, checking the landings, listening for footsteps. What frightened him most was the possibility that someone might be following him and he would not know until it was too late. He started arriving at work an hour early so he could park in the open lot three blocks away, even in winter rain.

The shame made the vigilance worse. When he caught himself scanning the parking lot during his lunch break, he would think: *This is what weak people do.* And then the memory would surface again—the concrete dust, the knife, his own silence—and the terror would spike, and he would need to check again, to be sure. He ruminated for hours about what he would do if he ever saw the man again, how he would hurt him, how he would make him pay. These fantasies gave him a brief sense of control, but they also kept the event vivid, and afterward he would try to push the whole thing out of his mind, telling himself to stop being ridiculous.

The checking and avoiding became a structure around his life. He stopped going to unfamiliar neighborhoods entirely—he could not assess the danger, could not know where the exits were, could not trust that he would be safe. When a meeting ran late or a client kept him waiting, he assumed something bad was happening: a breakdown in the system, a threat he had missed, a repeat of that moment when his life had stopped being his own. His wife noticed that he had become short-tempered, that he no longer wanted to go to the grocery store with her, that he spent his evenings staring at the television without watching it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday morning in the office supply closet. He had needed a new notepad, and he had stood at the door for five minutes, unable to open it, his heart hammering, his mind filling with the image of the alcove. He had walked away and told his supervisor he was feeling unwell. That night, sitting in his car in the driveway, he realized he could not keep living this way—afraid of a closet, afraid of a hallway, afraid of his own thoughts. He wanted to stop checking. He wanted to stop planning revenge. He wanted to be able to remember what happened without falling apart. But he was not sure he knew how.
